analysis_pieces.title: How do pubs make money? (9fin Educational, 13-Aug-2026)
analysis_pieces.key_findings: Sector-wide piece comparing the UK's four largest pubcos (Stonegate, Punch, Greene King, M&B). Punch is the most freehold-heavy (92% of 1,298-1,310 pubs on freehold/long-leasehold), has fully exited whole-business securitisation, and is structurally insulated from National Living Wage/NIC increases because its L&T tenants and Pub Partnership operators - not Punch itself - bear labour costs. Punch's LTV was 64% (Aug-2025) versus Stonegate's ~88% (H1 26, lease-adjusted). Stonegate is the most leveraged (7.9x H1 26) and structurally complex (Unique WBS plus an unrestricted Platinum Group), with revenue falling 6.9% YoY in H1 26 and only marginal disposal progress (GBP52m of proceeds against GBP3.7bn of debt); management there has 'stated a clear path to deleveraging' but progress is described as marginal. Debt maturities across all four pubcos run 2029-35, so 9fin's own view is that no operator in this sub-sector faces a genuine near-term refinancing wall. Punch's 7.875% 2030 SSNs were quoted at 2.2% spread-to-worst / 6.6% YTW versus Stonegate's 10.75% 2029 SSNs at 5.6% STW - the pricing gap itself signals the market differentiates sharply between the two credits. Sector-wide cost themes flagged: National Living Wage rose 4.1% to GBP12.71/hr from April 2026, NIC rose from 13.8% to 15% from April 2025 (c.GBP2,500 additional annual cost per FTE for operators that bear labour directly); nearly two pubs a day closed in Q1 2026; Gen Z drinking materially less (structural, not cyclical). A 20% cut to business rates for pubs was announced by government in July 2026 (partial offset).

analysis_pieces.title: Punch Pubs - Credit QuickTake (9fin, 20-May-2025)
analysis_pieces.key_findings: Seventh-largest UK pub operator (1,264 sites at the time), 90% wet-led, 81% suburban/community. LTM sales GBP326.7m, pro forma run-rate adjusted underlying EBITDA GBP111m (34% margin) as of Feb-2025. Strategic shift from Leased & Tenanted to the higher-EBITDA Pub Partnership model continuing (PP is 25% of pubs but ~40% of EBITDA). Between 2020 and Feb-2025, Punch disposed of 172 pubs for GBP92.6m net proceeds at a 21.4x EBITDA multiple, evidencing disposal optionality from its freehold base. Key risks flagged: earnings volatility from the PP shift (loses the stability of L&T rental income, ~GBP28m/year), execution risk on the L&T-to-PP conversion pipeline, wet-led exposure to changing consumer/health trends, 100% UK geographic concentration, and supplier concentration (Carlsberg-Britvic ~31% of drinks supply costs).

analysis_pieces.title: Punch Pubs - Bond Legal QuickTake (9fin, 20-May-2025)
analysis_pieces.key_findings: Covers the 2025 refinancing of the GBP600m 2026 SSNs into the GBP640m 7.875% SSNs due Dec-2030. Senior secured leverage covenant threshold (SSNL) set at 6.5x, described by 9fin's legal team as 'punchy' but in line with the prior 2021 notes. Super Senior RCF (GBP85m) expected undrawn at issuance, plus day-one capacity for a further GBP15m of incremental super senior debt. No non-guarantor debt cap, but high initial guarantor coverage (day one Guarantors represented 97.7% of revenue / 98.5% of Adjusted Underlying EBITDA). J.Crew blocker included, limiting (but not eliminating) drop-down/asset-stripping risk to Material IP. Security is a first-priority equitable charge over the freehold estate; the RCF ranks super senior. No maintenance financial covenant tied to RCF utilisation is captured in 9fin's covenant extraction for this instrument (unlike some comparable UK consumer credits) - this appears to be an incurrence-only covenant package typical of a straightforward HY bond, with any springing test (if one exists) likely to sit in the separate RCF facility agreement, which is not in 9fin's document set.

analysis_pieces.title: Restructuring the Watchlist - Legal Analysis of European Distressed Tracker, September 2026 (9fin, 23-Sep-2026)
analysis_pieces.key_findings: 9fin's own monthly distress tracker for September 2026 adds five names (Awaze, Iberconsa, Hilding Anders, Landal, Wagamama). Neither Punch nor Stonegate appears among this month's additions to the Watchlist or In Progress categories. This is a useful, independent cross-check: as of the most current 9fin distress screening available, Punch is not flagged by 9fin's own restructuring desk, and no new addition for Stonegate is recorded this month either (though Stonegate's underlying credit metrics - see news table - are weaker and it may already sit on an earlier month's list, which was not in scope of this pull).

situation_overview: Punch Pubs is a UK community pub operator (1,310 pubs as of the 40 weeks to 17-May-26) owned by Fortress Investment Group since December 2021. The business is 90% drink-led and skewed to suburban/community sites, insulating it from the high-street, late-night and destination-dining pressures affecting managed operators. Trading has improved consistently through FY26: revenue for the 40 weeks to 17-May-26 was GBP274.7m (+9.1% YoY), underlying EBITDA was GBP75.9m (+6.6% YoY), and the subsequent Q3 FY26 earnings flash (to end-July) showed sales +8.6% YoY and EBITDA +5.8% YoY, with net leverage improving 0.1x to 6.6x on a secured basis (7.3x on an IFRS 16 basis per 9fin's financial database). Growth has been driven by like-for-like price/volume gains, continued conversion of pubs from the Leased & Tenanted model to the higher-margin Pub Partnership model (60 conversions in the 40-week period versus 22 a year earlier), and bolt-on freehold acquisitions (50 pubs for GBP36.2m in the period, funded from a GBP50m private tap of the 2030 notes priced at a premium in February 2026). Quarter four trading to 12-Jul-26 was described by management as strong, with an additional boost from elevated England World Cup viewing (Pub Partnership like-for-like sales +59% over the seven England match days). Group loan-to-value stood at 62.8% as of 17-May-26 (property assets GBP1,079.4m against net debt of GBP677.4m), reflecting the Savills-valued, 92%-freehold-or-long-leasehold estate. The GBP640m (now GBP690m after the tap) 7.875% Senior Secured Notes were only refinanced in June 2025 and mature Dec-2030; the GBP85m super senior RCF was fully undrawn as at the Q3 FY26 balance sheet date. The one credit-relevant management change this year is at CFO level: Matt Ward (ex-CFO, Village Hotels; prior senior finance roles at Greene King) took over as CFO on 11-May-26, with 15-year incumbent Steve Dando moving into a newly created Chief Financial Strategist role rather than departing outright - a retention-oriented transition rather than a distress signal. Near-term outlook, per management's own commentary on the Q2 FY26 call, is for continued benefit from like-for-like growth, Pub Partnership conversions, bolt-on M&A and cost optimisation, with no mention of refinancing pressure, covenant concerns or trading deterioration.

sector_context.creditor_comment_assessment: The creditor's characterisation of pubs as 'struggling' is best read as a sector-wide narrative driven primarily by Stonegate and by macro cost pressures, not as a Punch-specific signal. Stonegate (TDR Capital) is the clearer distress story: Q3 FY26 (18-Sep-26) showed sales -8.6% YoY, net leverage still at 8.1x (versus Punch's 6.6x), an ~88% lease-adjusted LTV (versus Punch's 62.8%), a CCC+ Fitch rating (affirmed 09-Jul-26) against Punch's B3/B- CFR, a whole-business-securitisation-plus-unrestricted-subsidiary structure that 9fin's own legal team has flagged as complex, and, as of 23-Sep-26, reported talks with Heineken to sell hundreds of pubs 'as debts mount' (Food Manufacturer). Stonegate is also under scrutiny for its treatment of tenants (The Times, 15-Jul-26). Beyond Stonegate specifically, there is a genuine sector-wide cost headwind: National Living Wage +4.1% and employer NIC +1.2pt took effect through 2025-26, adding an estimated GBP2,500 per FTE for operators that employ staff directly; nearly two pubs a day closed nationally in Q1 2026; and HM Treasury announced in August 2026 that it is reviewing business rates for pubs and hotels (following a partially offsetting 20% business rates cut for pubs announced in July 2026). These pressures are real, but they bite hardest on managed/food-led operators who directly employ staff and carry higher fixed costs (Greene King, M&B, and Stonegate's remaining managed estate) - not on Punch, whose 90%-drink-led, independently-operated model means staffing costs sit with tenants and Pub Partnership operators, not with Punch itself.
sector_context.freehold_resilience: Freehold ownership is the single clearest differentiator identified across the sector research. Punch is the most freehold-heavy of the four major UK pubcos (92% freehold/long-leasehold), giving it (i) a materially lower LTV (62.8%) and therefore more headroom before any property revaluation or lending-market stress becomes binding, (ii) demonstrated disposal optionality - GBP92.6m of net proceeds from 172 pub disposals between 2020 and Feb-2025 at a 21.4x EBITDA multiple - that leaseholders do not have, and (iii) an asset base (Savills-valued at GBP1,079.4m against GBP690m of secured notes) that materially over-collateralises the debt stack. Stonegate, by contrast, carries ~88% lease-adjusted LTV and has made only marginal disposal progress relative to its ~GBP3.7-3.8bn of gross debt, and its Platinum Pubs freehold portfolio (944 tied plus 90 free-of-tie pubs) was carved out into an unrestricted subsidiary in Jan-2024 rather than retained and monetised within the restricted group - reducing, not adding to, direct creditor recourse to that freehold value. In short: freehold ownership at Punch is a source of resilience and refinancing/disposal flexibility; the wider sector narrative of stress is concentrated in operators (Stonegate in particular) with higher leverage, higher LTV, and more encumbered or securitised structures.

No indication of cash burn; operating cash flow for the 40-week period was GBP64.1m. covenants.metric: Senior Secured Net Leverage Ratio (SSNL) - incurrence covenant gating further ratio debt/RP capacity, not a periodic maintenance test
covenants.current_level: 6.6x (secured, Q3 FY26 per 9fin financials) / 6.4x-6.9x net leverage across FY23-FY25 on a declining trend
covenants.trigger_level: 6.5x (no-worse-than test for incurring further ratio debt under the notes indenture)
covenants.test_date: Tested only on incurrence of new debt/restricted payments, not on a fixed periodic date; RCF is fully undrawn so no springing maintenance covenant (if one exists in the separate RCF facility agreement, which 9fin's document set does not cover) is currently live
covenants.assessment: Actual leverage (6.6x) currently sits marginally above the 6.5x incurrence gate, which would restrict Punch's ability to incur further ratio debt or make certain restricted payments outside existing baskets - a capacity constraint, not a default or maintenance breach. This is not, on the evidence available, a covenant trip.

recommendation.rationale: None of the three key triggers is present or clearly approaching for Punch Pubs on the evidence gathered. Liquidity is stable and improving (GBP97.6m available, RCF fully undrawn, up from GBP94.0m at FY25 year-end). The GBP690m 2030 notes were only refinanced in June 2025 and mature in December 2030 (c.51 months out), well outside the 18-24 month maturity-wall window CLAUDE.md flags for concern, and the company has demonstrated continued capital markets access on favourable terms (the Feb-2026 GBP50m tap priced at a premium to fund accretive bolt-on M&A, not to plug a liquidity gap). Leverage (6.6x secured / 7.3x IFRS 16) sits marginally above the 6.5x incurrence-covenant gate in the notes, which constrains further debt incurrence and restricted payments but is not a maintenance covenant and is not in breach; leverage has in fact been on a declining trend since FY22 (7.7x) and improved further intra-quarter in Q3 FY26. The creditor's 'struggling' comment is better explained by the wider UK pub/consumer-discretionary narrative - specifically Stonegate's much higher leverage (8.1x), higher LTV (~88%), CCC+ rating, tenant-treatment scrutiny and reported Heineken sale talks 'as debts mount' - and by sector-wide National Living Wage/NIC/business-rates cost inflation that disproportionately affects managed, food-led and heavily leased operators. Punch's freehold-heavy (92%), drink-led, independently-operated model is structurally insulated from most of that specific cost pressure, and 9fin's own September 2026 distress tracker does not add Punch (or, this month, Stonegate) to its restructuring watchlist. The one material development since the 27-Sep-2026 assessment is a CFO transition (Matt Ward replacing Steve Dando, effective 11-May-2026), which reads as a planned succession rather than a distress signal. Recommendation: maintain 'Pass', but monitor sector cost inflation (NLW/NIC/business rates outcome of the Treasury review announced Aug-2026) and Stonegate's Heineken process as a leading indicator for the broader UK pub sub-sector, given Punch's comparative resilience could still be tested if cost pressures broaden or consumer spend deteriorates further.
triggers: None of the three triggers (covenant trip, unrefinanceable maturity/leverage wall, liquidity issue) is currently present or clearly approaching for Punch Pubs specifically. Sector-level cost/consumer-spend pressure is noted as a watch item, concentrated in peer Stonegate rather than in Punch.
